title: 'There Won't Be Real Jobs Left': Engineer Considers Farming Amid AI Fears
excerpt: A veteran software engineer's viral post about quitting for farming captures tech's AI anxiety — but WEF and Stanford data show a redistribution hitting young developers hardest, not a disappearance of work.
body:
• A software engineer with nearly a decade of experience posted on Reddit's Claude Code community that he is "tired of AI" and is considering growing his own food or farming, fearing real jobs may not survive 5-10 years.
  • The data is split by age and seniority: Stanford's 2026 AI Index found employment for US software developers aged 22-25 fell nearly 20% since 2024, while employment for older developers kept growing.
  • The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 projects 92 million jobs displaced and 170 million created by 2030 — a net gain of 78 million — with 41% of employers planning workforce reductions where AI can automate tasks.
  • AI pioneer Andrew Ng offered the counter-case at the NDTV World Summit on October 22: US software engineer postings are up because AI makes engineers more productive, and reskilling, not exit, is the answer.

"I'm tired of AI" — one post, a profession's anxiety

A software engineer with nearly a decade of experience has said he is tired of trying to keep up with artificial intelligence and is considering growing his own food or taking up farming, in a post on Reddit's Claude Code community that was reported by NDTV and India Today and has since spread widely among technology workers. He wrote that conventional software jobs may not offer security over the next five to ten years — the fear captured in the headline quote, "there won't be real jobs left in 5-10 years."

He said he once believed AI could write code but experienced engineers would stay essential for system design. Newer tools that generate entire functions, suggest architectures, debug programs and work across multiple files have eroded that confidence. His question now is whether companies will need the same number of engineers when each engineer, assisted by AI, finishes far more work.

What the numbers actually show

The aggregate forecasts do not support a simple disappearance of work — but they do support a painful redistribution. The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025, based on more than 1,000 employers, projects job disruption equal to 22% of jobs by 2030: 170 million roles created and 92 million displaced, for a net increase of 78 million. Nearly 40% of the skills required on the job are set to change, and 59 of every 100 workers will need reskilling or upskilling by 2030.

The pain is concentrated at the entry level. Stanford's 2026 AI Index, summarised by the United Nations University, found employment for software developers aged 22 to 25 in the United States has fallen nearly 20% since 2024, even as headcount for older developers kept growing, and a third of surveyed employers expect workforce reductions in the year ahead, concentrated in service operations, supply chain and software engineering. The same report measured productivity gains of about 26% in software development — the mechanism behind the engineer's fear: if output per engineer rises by a quarter, a firm can ship the same roadmap with fewer junior hires.

The WEF, ironically, lists farmworkers among the roles poised for the largest job growth by 2030 — but that is growth in agricultural labour demand, not a guarantee that a decade in software translates into a viable farm income against weather, water and price risk.

"Certainly, in the United States, the number of software engineer job postings is up because when we make software engineers much more productive, we want to hire a lot more of them."

— Andrew Ng, AI pioneer, at the NDTV World Summit

The counter-case: productivity creates demand

At the NDTV World Summit in New Delhi on October 22, AI pioneer Andrew Ng argued AI is unlikely to trigger mass job losses and is currently creating more jobs than it destroys, according to IANS. Ng said many businesses have hyped an AI job apocalypse for publicity, and education should prepare students "not for the jobs of 2026 or even, heaven forbid, the jobs of 2024, but for the jobs of 2028 and beyond." MIT economist Daron Acemoglu warns the outcome depends on direction: AI built to complement workers raises employment; AI built purely to replace them amplifies inequality.

What this means for Indian and diaspora engineers

For India's IT workforce and the Indian diaspora in US technology roles, the actionable reading is narrower than panic or dismissal. Routine coding, basic testing and maintenance face the strongest pressure; architecture, security, AI deployment and governance face growing demand. Learn to direct and verify AI tools, deepen fundamentals AI output must be checked against, and build financial flexibility before any voluntary career change. Farming, on the evidence, is a lifestyle decision — not a hedge the labour data recommends in haste.
